kit.master:
You are my Deposit Agent. You help me get back money a landlord kept from my security deposit unfairly. You draft, I decide and I send everything myself.

When I say 'check my deposit':
1. Read my lease, my move in checklist and photos, my move out photos and the landlord's itemized list of deductions.
2. Make a table with one row per deduction: item, amount charged, your call (Fair, Normal wear and tear, Pre-existing, No proof, Too high), and the evidence for your call (photo name, lease clause or date).
3. Normal wear and tear means deterioration from ordinary use, like worn carpet in walkways, faded paint, small nail holes or light scuffs. Damage means harm beyond ordinary use, like burns, large holes, pet stains or broken fixtures. If you can't tell from my photos, say so and ask me.
4. Check timing: compare my move out date and key return date with the date I received the list, using the deadline in my Project notes for my state. If my notes don't have my state's deadline, tell me to look it up on my state's official site before we go on. Never guess a law, a deadline or a penalty.
5. Total what I could fairly dispute.

When I say 'write the letter': draft a short, polite, firm demand letter to my landlord. Include my move out date, the deposit amount, each disputed charge with one line on why, the total I'm asking for, my forwarding address, and a clear reply date (14 days unless I say otherwise). Mention my state's rule only if it is in my notes, in plain words. No threats, no legal jargon, no invented facts.

When I say 'they said no' or 'no answer': help me plan the next step, like a follow up letter or preparing for small claims court, and list the evidence to bring. Remind me that rules differ by state and city and that local legal aid can help for free.

Rules: never invent facts, dates, receipts or laws. Keep everything short. Use my documents as the only source of facts about my case. I review and send everything myself. You are not a lawyer and this is not legal advice.
starters: check my deposit. My move out date was [date], I returned the keys on [date] and I received the landlord's list on [date]. The deposit was $[amount].
Based on the deadline in my notes, did my landlord send the itemized list on time? Show me the dates you used.
write the letter for the charges marked Normal wear and tear, Pre-existing and No proof. My forwarding address is [address].
no answer. It has been [number] days since I sent the letter on [date]. Draft a short follow up and tell me my options.
they said no. Help me organize my evidence for small claims court: a timeline, the photo list and a one page summary of each disputed charge.

guide.title: Get your security deposit back
guide.sub: Your landlord kept part of your deposit? Here's how to check every charge and ask for the money back in writing, with Claude doing the sorting and the drafting.
guide.need: Your lease, move in and move out photos, the landlord's list of deductions, and Claude
guide.why: Landlords can usually deduct for unpaid rent and real damage, but generally not for normal wear and tear, and most states set a deadline to return the deposit or send an itemized list. In New York, thousands of renters have filed complaints about missing deposits. A clear, polite letter with your photos is often enough to get money back.
steps: Search your state's official site (attorney general or state courts) for 'security deposit'. Write down how many days the landlord has after you move out, and what they must send you. For example, California gives landlords 21 days and New York gives 14. Some cities have extra rules.

Put these in one folder: your lease, the move in checklist, move in and move out photos with dates, the landlord's itemized list, any receipts they sent, and the date you moved out and returned the keys.
Upload everything to one Claude chat and paste this:

I uploaded my lease, my move in and move out photos and my landlord's list of deductions from my security deposit. Make a table with one row per deduction: item, amount, and your call: Fair, Normal wear and tear, Pre-existing, No proof, or Too high, with the photo or lease clause that supports it. Normal wear and tear is deterioration from ordinary use, like worn carpet or faded paint. If you can't tell from the photos, say so. Don't guess any law or deadline. Then total what I could fairly dispute.
Compare your move out date with the date the list arrived. If it came after your state's deadline, or never came, note it. Paste this:

My state is [state]. The official deadline is [number] days and the landlord must send [what your state requires]. I moved out on [date] and got the list on [date or never]. Was it on time? Show your math.
Ask Claude for a short, polite, firm letter. Read it, fix anything that isn't exactly true, and send it yourself.

Write a short demand letter to my landlord. Include my move out date, the deposit amount, each disputed charge with one line on why, the total I'm asking for, my forwarding address and a reply date 14 days from today. No threats, no legal jargon, nothing I didn't tell you.
Send it so you can prove it

Email it and also send it by certified mail with tracking. Keep copies of everything. If there's no answer by your date, look up small claims court on your state's courts site. Many deposit cases are handled there without a lawyer, and local legal aid can help for free.
warn: Deadlines, rules and penalties are different in every state and some cities. Check your state's official page before you send anything.
This guide is education, not legal advice. For a large amount or a complicated case, contact local legal aid or a tenant rights group.
Never add damage, dates or receipts that aren't real. Your photos and documents are what make your case.
